newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. trustbusters to soothe EU bruises.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. trustbusters to soothe EU bruises.

text.p: President Bill Clinton praised the European Union's tentative approval Wednesday of Boeing Co.'s acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp. as American antitrust officials moved to patch up bruised relations with their European counterparts.
"I am pleased that Boeing and the EU have resolved their differences. We hope that the EU will give the merger final approval expeditiously," Clinton said in a written statement.
"The Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger will promote consolidation and efficiency in the U.S. defence industry and preserve the jobs of 14,000 workers at Douglas Aircraft Co."

While the EU decision appeared to mark a foreign policy victory for the president, he said nothing about the European consortium Airbus Industrie, which many U.S. politicians blamed for the EU's reluctance to approve the deal.

In fact, American politicians excoriated the EU and held out the U.S. Federal Trade Commission as the proper forum for consideration of the deal. The FTC cleared the $15 billion merger earlier this month.

But the two top antitrust officials in the United States looked to reinforce the traditional cooperation that has marked the enforcement of competition policy, after a crisis that put their relationship with the EU at risk.

The assistant attorney general in charge of antitrust, Joel Klein, who met in Brussels, Belgium, with the Europeans on behalf of the administration, said the two sides needed to learn to work together better.

"When you have an experience that is stressful and difficult, (you need) to make sure you learn what you can and see if you can avoid those kinds of problems in the future," he said in a telephone interview.
Federal Trade Commission Chairman Robert Pitofsky took pains to point out similarities in outlook between the EU and FTC on the Boeing deal.

Pitofsky said the EU "agreed with the essential point that led a majority of the FTC to clear the deal -- that Douglas no longer constituted a competitive force in selling large commerical planes to airlines."
Like the European Union, the Federal Trade Commission also found troublng the exclusive provider contracts Boeing had with three airlines.

But while the Europeans made the agreements a sticking point under their law, American legal precedents say that if exclusive contracts amount to less than 30 percent of a market, they are not a problem.
In this case, the exclusive contracts amounted to between 11 percent and 12 percent of business.
"They have a differrent law and different precedents," said Pitofsky.
